cardio-wb-cardio0-q83.html:
From 09 - Endocarditis (atherosclerosis risk factors). The lecture's major non-modifiable risk factors are older age, male sex (estrogen is protective) and family history. Smoking is a major modifiable one. So A, B and C are all risk factors.

Family history only counts when the disease is premature in a first-degree relative: male under 55, female under 65. That cut-off comes from the key; the lecture only says "50-60s".

  • D: the father died at 65, past the male cut-off, so this is not premature CAD and it is the answer.
  • E: the mother died at 51, under 65, so it counts.

cardio-wb-cardio0-q24.html:
From 05 - Aortic Regurgitation. AR comes from either the leaflets or the aortic root. The lecture's leaflet causes include rheumatic heart disease (A), bicuspid and other congenital valves (E), endocarditis, and connective-tissue and inflammatory disease such as lupus, ankylosing spondylitis and rheumatoid arthritis (C). Root causes are idiopathic ectasia, hypertension, Marfan and bicuspid aortopathy.

  • LV dilation (D) is a consequence of chronic AR: volume overload dilates the LV. It is not a cause of AR. (A dilated LV causes secondary mitral regurgitation.)
  • Endocarditis (B) is the classic cause of acute AR, but the lecture also lists it among the leaflet causes.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The workbook keys B, endocarditis, presumably because endocarditis is the textbook cause of acute AR. But 05 - Aortic Regurgitation (and 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease) list endocarditis among the leaflet causes of AR. Left ventricular dilation is never a cause of AR, only its result. The answer the material supports is D.

cardio-w3-new-q3-3.html:
From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. The culprit artery sets the wall that infarcts:

  • LAD (I) - anterior MI (C): ST elevation in the anterior leads V3-V4 (V1-V6 if it extends septal and lateral). The LAD supplies the anterior wall and the anterior two-thirds of the septum.
  • RCA (II) - inferior MI (A): ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with reciprocal depression in I and aVL. In the 85% who are right-dominant, the RCA gives the posterior descending artery.
  • Left circumflex (III) - posterior MI (B): often missed on a 12-lead. Look for ST depression in V1-V3 or add V8-V9.

cardio-w3-new-q4-4.html:
From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. A STEMI that is not reperfused evolves through a fixed sequence, which the key A-E-F-B-D-C traces through the panels:

  • Normal baseline.
  • Hyperacute T waves: broad, peaked, asymmetric. These come first and precede ST elevation.
  • ST elevation: transmural injury in the ischemic zone.
  • Q waves develop as necrosis spreads from subendocardium to epicardium and the wall becomes full-thickness infarct.
  • ST normalises, T inverts.
  • ST and T normal, Q wave persists for life.

A Q wave means necrosis, not ischemia, which is why it is the last thing to go and never does.

flags.title: Only partly covered by the notes
flags.html: 04 - Myocardial Infarction covers ST elevation during ischemia and the permanent Q wave after full-thickness infarction, and the hyperacute T wave feature note places those T waves before ST elevation. No lecture note lays out the full six-stage sequence. The middle stages above are from general principles, and the letters could not be checked against the panels, which are unlabelled in the bank.

cardio-w3-new-q5-5.html:
From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. The lecture splits contraindications to thrombolysis into absolute and relative. The absolute ones include:

  • Any prior intracranial bleed (C), however long ago.
  • Ischemic stroke within 3 months (D): 2 months qualifies. After 3 months it becomes relative.
  • Intracranial malignancy (E).

The others:

  • Pregnancy (A) and therapeutic anticoagulation with warfarin (B): relative contraindications.
  • BP 160/90 (F): not a contraindication at all. Only BP > 180/110 is, and even that is relative.

The other absolute ones are closed head or facial trauma within 3 months, active bleeding (except menses), and aortic dissection or acute pericarditis.

cardio-wb-cardio0-q82.html:
From 02 - Imaging in Cardiovascular Disease. The lecture singles out left ventricular function as the strong predictor of outcome and survival. LVEF is normal above 50%, and prognosis falls once it drops below 30-35%. 04 - Myocardial Infarction shows 6-month mortality climbing steeply below an LVEF of about 45%. After an MI, echo or MUGA to assess LV function is the test that best predicts long-term survival.

  • Framingham (A): estimates the risk of developing CAD in people without it.
  • Angiography (C): shows anatomy. The amount of myocardium lost predicts outcome better.
  • Age (D): a risk factor, but weaker than LVEF.

cardio-wb-cardio0-q101.html:
From 05 - Complications of Acute MI. All four are on the lecture's list of MI complications:

  • Heart failure (A): early as pulmonary edema or cardiogenic shock, especially after a large anterior (proximal LAD) MI, and late from remodeling.
  • Pulmonary edema (B): an early mechanical complication, graded by Killip class.
  • Cardiac tamponade (C): LV free-wall rupture into the pericardium after a large transmural MI with late presentation. Usually fatal.
  • Acute MR (D): papillary muscle ischemia or rupture, typically posteromedial after an inferior MI. It gives a soft apical pansystolic murmur.

04 - Myocardial Infarction groups the same complications as ischemic, mechanical, arrhythmic and pericardial.

gi-w10-new-q17-17.html:
From 11 - Nausea, Vomiting, and Gastroparesis, and the antiemetic chart in 08. Cytotoxic drugs act as blood-borne emetics and local irritants on the CTZ and gut afferents. The lecture treats that pathway with 5-HT3 antagonists, dopamine antagonists, anticholinergics and cannabinoid agonists.

  • A. Ondansetron: the chart's first indication for 5-HT3 antagonists is chemotherapy-induced N/V.
  • B. Nabilone: its listed indication is chemotherapy-induced N/V, though not first line.
  • D. Domperidone: a D2 antagonist acting at the CTZ, which lies outside the blood-brain barrier.
  • C. Benzodiazepines treat nausea from higher cortical centres, such as anticipatory nausea on the drive to the hospital, not the drug-driven pathway itself.
  • E. Diclectin is the pregnancy agent.

gi-w10-new-q19-19.html:
From the GERD section of the GI summary notes (the alarm-feature list behind 09 - GERD). Alarm features are the ones that raise concern for cancer or a complication and send the patient to endoscopy. The list includes new dyspepsia at 60 or older, GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena), iron-deficiency anemia, anorexia or weight loss, dysphagia, odynophagia, persistent vomiting, and a first-degree relative with GI cancer.

  • A, B, C and D are all on that list.
  • E. Dental cavities come from acid erosion of enamel. That is an atypical presentation: it shows where refluxed acid reaches, but it says nothing about malignancy or a complication.

gi-w10-new-q2-2:
From 01 - Overview of the GI Tract. The four core processes run through the whole lecture:

  • Digestion (A): mechanical and chemical, starting in the mouth, with the stomach as the main site.
  • Motility (B): coordinated by the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus.
  • Secretion (D): regulated by the submucosal (Meissner) plexus.
  • Absorption (E): mostly in the small intestine, with water absorbed in the colon.

C. Regurgitation is not a function. It is a symptom, the effortless backflow of gastric contents when the lower esophageal sphincter is too relaxed, as in GERD (02 - Gastrointestinal Motility).

gi-w10-new-q20-20.html:
From 09 - GERD, with 04 - Esophageal Dysphagia.

  • C. True. Esophageal manometry measures esophageal pressures, including LES pressure. It is used in refractory GERD or diagnostic uncertainty.
  • A. False. Endoscopy does NOT diagnose GERD and cannot rule it out: 70% of patients have non-erosive disease with a normal-looking mucosa. It screens for complications and alternative diagnoses.
  • B. False. Manometry is exactly how motility disorders are diagnosed. The dysphagia lecture notes that endoscopy does not help much for them.
  • D. False as keyed. The option is garbled as written. The lecture lists ambulatory pH studies as a tool for refractory cases or diagnostic uncertainty, and nothing in it supports the claim.
  • E. False. Barrett's risk factors are an indication for endoscopy. Barrett's is a tissue diagnosis, not a clinical one.

gi-w10-new-q23-23:
From 07 - GI Imaging. The lecture's first ultrasound indication is evaluating solid organs such as the liver, spleen and kidney, along with fluid-filled structures (gallbladder, biliary tree) and ascites. The pancreas is the exception, because it lies deep behind bowel gas.

  • A. A full abdominal ultrasound takes about 30 minutes, so it is a poor choice when time is the constraint.
  • B. Large body habitus is a listed disadvantage: extra fat scatters the sound waves.
  • D. Very good spatial resolution belongs to CT, not ultrasound, which is also operator-dependent.
gi-w10-new-q24-24:
From 07 - GI Imaging. The lecture's obstruction signs on an abdominal series are dilated bowel, differential air-fluid levels, string of pearls, step-ladder pattern, gasless abdomen, and no air beyond the obstructed segment.

  • D inverts the last sign. Gas cannot pass the blockage, so the bowel beyond it is empty, while the bowel before it dilates. “Air only beyond” is the opposite of what you see.
  • A, B and C are genuine signs. String of pearls is specific to small-bowel obstruction.
  • E fails because D is not a sign.
gi-w10-new-q8-8:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Anterior Abdominal Wall. As the testis descends through the inguinal canal it takes a sleeve from each layer it passes through, and those sleeves become the three coverings of the spermatic cord:

  • A. Transversalis fascia becomes the internal spermatic fascia, at the deep ring.
  • B. Internal oblique becomes the cremaster muscle and fascia.
  • C. External oblique becomes the external spermatic fascia, at the superficial ring.

D. Transversus abdominis contributes no layer. The canal passes beneath its arching lower fibres rather than through them, and its aponeurosis instead forms part of the canal's posterior wall as the conjoint tendon.

gi-wb-gi0-q51.html:
From 07 - Functional Gut Disorders. Before calling dyspepsia functional, the lecture has you check for red flags: dysphagia, vomiting, nocturnal pain, GI bleeding or anemia, an abdominal mass, weight loss, and onset after age 40.

  • B. Vomiting is on the list, because persistent emesis suggests obstruction, such as gastric outlet obstruction from an ulcer or a tumour.
  • A. Age matters at the older end, so onset under 12 is not a flag.
  • C. Nausea, D. heartburn and belching, and E. upper abdominal pain are the ordinary symptoms of dyspepsia and reflux. They are what brings the patient in, not warnings.

gi-w11-new-q10-10.html:
From 06 - Constipation. Rome IV functional constipation needs ≥ 2 of 6 features for the last 3 months, with onset ≥ 6 months before diagnosis, plus loose stools rarely present without laxatives and insufficient criteria for IBS. Shelby has < 3 spontaneous BMs per week (1-2) and incomplete evacuation in > 25%, which makes two features. She has had symptoms for 8 months, and she never has loose stools without laxatives. So no further criterion is needed.

  • A, B, D are additional features she does not need. A's threshold is also misquoted: the criterion is > 25%, not 1/3.
  • C is a required criterion (see the flag).

flags.title: The key assumes Shelby does not meet IBS criteria
flags.html: “Insufficient criteria for IBS” is itself part of the Rome IV definition in the lecture. The stem never mentions abdominal pain, so E is correct only if you read that absence as meaning the IBS criterion is met. Option C names a criterion she must still satisfy.

gi-w11-new-q13-13:
From 09 - Pharmacology of Prokinetics and Antidiarrheal Drugs. Serotonin promotes gut motility. Prucalopride (the stem misspells it) is a gut-selective 5-HT4 agonist, so it relieves constipation, and diarrhea is its expected side effect.

  • D2 antagonists are metoclopramide (crosses the BBB, extrapyramidal effects) and domperidone (does not, but prolongs QT).
  • A D2 agonist would slow the gut. It is not a prokinetic.
  • Cholinergic agonists increase contraction without coordination, which is why the lecture says prokinetics must act upstream.
  • The macrolide is erythromycin, a motilin agonist.
gi-w11-new-q14-14:
From 09 - Pharmacology of Prokinetics and Antidiarrheal Drugs. The lecture classes bismuth subsalicylate as an antisecretory agent (A): it stimulates fluid and electrolyte absorption across the gut wall. It has antimicrobial actions (C): it binds E. coli toxins and is part of quadruple H. pylori therapy. In the stomach's acid it forms salicylic acid, which inhibits PGE2 production, an anti-inflammatory effect (E).

  • Anticholinergic effects belong to diphenoxylate, which comes with atropine to deter overdose, not to bismuth.
  • Sympathetic activation is not part of any antidiarrheal mechanism in the lecture.

gi-w11-new-q16-16.html:
From 07 - Functional Gut Disorders. Diane (the previous question) has IBS with diarrhea. The lecture's IBS dietary management is: avoid caffeine for anxiety and diarrhea (B); increase soluble fibre, which helps both IBS-C and IBS-D (C); and try a low-FODMAP diet short term (A), because FODMAPs are osmotic and fermented. Regular routines (sleep, activity) are part of the same education, and regular meals (D) fits that. It is also the key's choice, though the lecture does not list meals by name.

  • E: reducing soluble fibre is the opposite of the lecture's advice. The target in the IBD overview chart is 20-25 g a day of psyllium-type fibre.

flags.title: Option D is not in the lecture
flags.html: The Functional Gut Disorders lecture does not mention scheduled meals. Option D is supported only by general principles of IBS routine. Verify it before relying on it.

gi-w11-new-q17-17:
From 07 - Functional Gut Disorders. The lecture's dyspepsia red flags are dysphagia, vomiting, nocturnal pain, GI bleeding or anemia, an abdominal mass, weight loss, and age of onset > 40. Any of these means you investigate (endoscopy) before calling it functional.

  • Age of onset < 12 reverses the age flag. It is late onset that raises concern for malignancy, and the Luminal GI Malignancies lecture uses ≥ 60 for new dyspepsia.
  • Nausea, heartburn with belching, and upper abdominal pain are the ordinary symptoms of dyspepsia itself. They are not alarm features.
gi-w11-new-q18-18:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Midgut & Hindgut. Below the pectinate line, the anal canal comes from proctodeum ectoderm. It is lined by squamous epithelium, and its lymph drains to the superficial inguinal nodes. Above the line, lymph drains to the internal iliac nodes. So C is correct.

  • A: the SMA supplies the colon to about two-thirds of the way along the transverse colon, not only to the hepatic (right colic) flexure.
  • B: the duodenum (parts 2-4), ascending colon, descending colon and rectum are retroperitoneal.
  • D: thoracic, lumbar and sacral splanchnic nerves are sympathetic. Parasympathetic supply is the vagus (midgut) and the pelvic splanchnics, S2-S4 (hindgut).
gi-wb-gi0-q77:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Midgut & Hindgut. Below the pectinate line, the anal canal comes from proctodeum ectoderm. It is lined by squamous epithelium, and its lymph drains to the superficial inguinal nodes. Above the line, lymph drains to the internal iliac nodes. So C is correct.

  • A: the SMA supplies the colon to about two-thirds of the way along the transverse colon, not only to the hepatic (right colic) flexure.
  • B: the duodenum (parts 2-4), ascending colon, descending colon and rectum are retroperitoneal.
  • D: thoracic, lumbar and sacral splanchnic nerves are sympathetic. Parasympathetic supply is the vagus (midgut) and the pelvic splanchnics, S2-S4 (hindgut).
gi-w11-new-q25-25:
From 05 - Infectious Diarrhea and the IBD overview chart. Only toxin-producing strains of C. difficile cause disease. The lecture warns that the GDH immunoassay is positive for toxic and non-toxic strains, so confirmation needs evidence of toxin: the chart lists PCR for the C. difficile toxin gene.

  • Abdominal X-ray is for severe disease, looking for toxic megacolon. It does not identify the organism.
  • Colonoscopy (really sigmoidoscopy) can show pseudomembranes, but it is invasive and risks perforating an inflamed colon. It is not the confirmatory test.
  • Stool culture and sensitivity covers the other bacterial causes. It cannot tell a toxigenic C. difficile strain from a carrier strain.
gi-w12-new-q15-15:
From 09 - Pancreatic Diseases & Malignancies. Acute pancreatitis is autodigestion by activated pancreatic enzymes, and each enzyme leaves its own lesion, so all four options are features:

  • Edema (A): from microvascular leakage.
  • Fat necrosis (B): from lipase, forming chalky calcium soaps.
  • Hemorrhage (C): from elastase destroying vessel walls.
  • Parenchymal destruction (D): from trypsin.

An acute inflammatory reaction completes the picture.
gi-w12-new-q17-17:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease. IgG4-related chronic acalculous cholecystitis is one expression of a systemic disease:

  • True (A): tissue infiltrates of IgG4-producing plasma cells define it.
  • False (B): serum IgG4 is raised, which is how the systemic disease is recognised.
  • False (C): the infiltrates involve the gallbladder, the biliary tree (IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis, often with extrahepatic obstruction) and the pancreas, as well as other organs.
  • True (D): it can mimic gallbladder cancer, and so may be resected as one.

So A and D (E) is the only combination that holds.
gi-wb-gi0-q107:
From 03 - Approach to Abnormal Liver Enzymes. AST is found outside the liver (muscle, red cells, brain) and falls in mitochondria-heavy, alcoholic, ischemic or vascular injury; ALT is the more liver-specific enzyme and dominates in most inflammatory or metabolic hepatocellular injury. The lecture's lists sort each item:

  • i. NAFLD = A (ALT > AST): steatosis and NASH are ALT-predominant.
  • ii. Acute Budd-Chiari = B (AST > ALT): hepatic venous outflow obstruction behaves like ischemic or congestive injury.
  • iii. Alcoholic liver disease = B (AST > ALT): classically at 2:1 or more.
  • iv. Viral hepatitis = A (ALT > AST): acute or chronic.
  • v. Celiac disease = A (ALT > AST): a systemic cause of mild ALT elevation.
  • vi. Ischemic hepatitis = B (AST > ALT), grouped with congestive hepatopathy.

gi-w10-new-q1-1.html:
From 01 - Overview of the GI Tract. The lecture's sphincters each separate two compartments. The pyloric sphincter separates the stomach from the small intestine, meaning its first part, the duodenum. The jejunum begins only at the duodenojejunal junction, so C is the false description.

  • UES (A): oral cavity (pharynx) from esophagus. Correct.
  • LES (B): esophagus from stomach. Correct.
  • Ileocecal (D): terminal ileum from large intestine. Correct.

The internal and external anal sphincters complete the list, separating the large intestine from the outside.

gi-w10-new-q10-10.html:
From 10 - GI Secretion. Salivary secretion is controlled by the autonomic nervous system, not the ENS. The lecture's summary says that saliva is primarily under neural (autonomic) regulation, while gastric, pancreatic and biliary secretion depend more on hormones and paracrine signals. So B is false.

  • A is true, and a common trap: both arms stimulate. Parasympathetic input adds enzymes and water; sympathetic input adds mucin, which thickens the saliva.
  • C is true: sleep, fatigue, fear and dehydration all reduce secretion.
  • D is true: the parasympathetic drive is cholinergic, so anticholinergics cause a dry mouth, as the antihistamine side-effect list also shows.

gi-w10-new-q12-12.html:
From 10 - GI Secretion. The lecture names the three major mediators of gastric acid secretion: acetylcholine, histamine and gastrin. ACh (M3) acts on parietal cells directly and also releases histamine from ECL cells and gastrin from G cells. Histamine acts on H2 receptors in a paracrine way. Gastrin acts on CCK2 receptors, both on parietal cells and through ECL histamine release. PPIs block the final step of all three.

  • Somatostatin (A, B): an inhibitor. It is released by D cells when the pH falls below 3.
  • Pepsin (A): an enzyme activated by acid, not a driver of acid.
  • Epinephrine (D): not one of the lecture's stimulants of acid secretion.

gi-w10-new-q21-21.html:
From 08 - Anatomy of the Foregut. The descending colon is retroperitoneal. It is covered by peritoneum only on its front surface and is fixed to the posterior wall, because its mesentery fused with the parietal peritoneum when the gut returned from herniation. The retroperitoneal organs are the SAD PUCKER list: suprarenals, aorta/IVC, duodenum parts 2-4, pancreas, ureters, ascending and descending colon, kidneys, distal esophagus and rectum.

  • Spleen, stomach and ileum (A-C): intraperitoneal and mobile.
  • First part of the duodenum (E): the exception within the duodenum. It is foregut, intraperitoneal, and the site of most duodenal ulcers.

gi-w10-new-q22-22.html:
From 08 - Anatomy of the Hepatobiliary & Portal System. The gallbladder lies under the liver and drains through the cystic duct into the structures at the porta hepatis. The hepatic portal vein runs there, beside the common bile duct and the hepatic artery, and enters the liver at the porta. It is the large non-arterial vessel close to a cholecystectomy dissection (Calot's triangle, around the cystic artery).

  • Splenic, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric veins (A, C, D): they join to form the portal vein. That happens behind the pancreas, away from the gallbladder bed.
  • IVC (E): retroperitoneal. It receives the hepatic veins behind the liver, not in the gallbladder field.

review.t: Anatomy of the Hepatobiliary & Portal System

gi-w11-new-q11-11.html:
From 06 - Constipation. The lecture's red flags that call for colonoscopy in constipation are the CRC flags: hematochezia, anemia, weight loss, age over 50, a sudden change in bowel habits, and a family history of CRC. Fever is not on that list. In an adult it points toward an inflammatory or infectious process (e.g., diverticulitis, where colonoscopy is avoided in the acute phase), not toward occult malignancy.

  • Anemia (A), a sudden change in bowel habits (B), hematochezia (C) and age 50 (E) are all listed flags. The Choosing Wisely note adds the converse: do not scope for constipation under 50 without a family history or alarm features.

Fever does appear as a "systemic" red flag in the pediatric constipation chart. That list is for children.

gi-w11-new-q19-19.html:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Midgut & Hindgut. In the figure the transverse colon is lifted up and the small bowel has been removed. The labelled vessels are:

  • C. Right colic artery: an SMA branch running to the ascending colon on the right. The label and its pointer match, so this is the correct one.
  • A. "Middle colic": the pointer ends on the highlighted loop that runs along the inner edge of the transverse colon. That loop is the marginal artery (of Drummond), which runs the length of the colon. The middle colic is the SMA branch that heads up into the transverse mesocolon.
  • B. "Intestinal arcades": points at the same marginal loop beside the descending colon. The arcades are the loops in the small-bowel mesentery that feed the vasa recta.
  • D. "Celiac trunk": points at the descending colon wall. The celiac trunk is a foregut vessel above the pancreas not shown here.

flags.title: Diagram read at low resolution
flags.html: The bank's figure is small (about 250 px). The readings of where each pointer ends are my interpretation of it, and they agree with the key's C. If the prose and the image seem to disagree, trust the image.

flags.title: The answer options are missing
flags.html: The bank lists no options for this question. The letters A-D are the labels printed on the figure itself.

gi-w12-new-q16-16.html:
From the pancreas chart in 04 - Gallbladder Disease and 09 - Pancreatic Diseases & Malignancies. Each option is a treatment line in the lecture, so all of the above is right:

  • Stop alcohol (A): alcohol causes 70% of cases. Alcohol and smoking cessation are "important in management".
  • Treat malabsorption (B): pancreatic enzyme replacement and dietary fat restriction for the steatorrhea.
  • Treat pain (C): avoid alcohol and large meals, then non-narcotics, then narcotics (many patients end up on them), then stent or surgery (Puestow).
  • Replace nutritional deficiencies (D): fat-soluble vitamins and B12 are lost with exocrine failure.

gi-w12-new-q20-20.html:
From 01 - Approach to Liver Masses. The lecture supports the core of this. HCC is the most common primary liver cancer ("C = most Common primary liver tumour" in the ABCs). It is most common in males over 40, and 90% arise in cirrhotic livers (aflatoxin, hepatitis B or C, cirrhosis). That makes B and D true, and D's "aged 40" is the lecture's "over 40".

  • "Used to be called a hepatoma" (A): not stated in the notes. It is the older name for the tumour.
  • "#8 cause of death worldwide" (C): not in the notes either. It is the question writer's figure.

Because the key is E, A and C have to be accepted as true for this question.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: Only statements B and D are in the lecture notes. Neither "hepatoma" (A) nor "#8 cause of death worldwide" (C) appears anywhere in the notes. The reasoning for those two is not from the lectures, and the worldwide ranking in particular is an unsourced figure. Verify it before relying on it.

gi-w13-new-q15-15.html:
From 05 - Infectious Diarrhea (with 05 - Pediatric Diarrhea). Dehydration is the main complication of diarrhea, and infants are at higher risk. Rehydration should use a balanced electrolyte solution (ORS). Diarrhea loses water and sodium. Replacing that with plain water dilutes the remaining sodium, causing hyponatremia (the same reason tap-water enemas carry a hyponatremia warning in 06 - Constipation). Plain water also supplies no glucose to a child who is not eating, so hypoglycemia is a risk.

  • Taste preference (A): high-sugar drinks worsen osmotic diarrhea. They are not a reason to avoid water.
  • Dehydration is necessary (C): false. Correcting it is the most important treatment.
  • Nutrients for growth (D): ORS replaces fluid and electrolytes. It is not a nutritional supplement.

gi-wb-gi0-q89.html:
From 10 - Upper and Lower GI Bleeding. Active bleeding is a main indication for endoscopy, not a contraindication. After resuscitation, urgent EGD is "both diagnostic and therapeutic" (epinephrine injection, cautery, hemoclips, variceal banding). In lower GI bleeding, stable patients go on to colonoscopy.

  • Suspected perforation (A): insufflating air through a perforated viscus worsens the leak. Free air is a surgical emergency (04 - Abdominal Pain).
  • Obstruction (B): bowel prep cannot pass, and a distended bowel risks perforation.
  • Fixed or redundant colon (C): the scope cannot be advanced safely, which raises the perforation risk.
  • Recent MI (E): sedation and the procedure put stress on an unstable heart.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: The notes support D: bleeding is an indication for endoscopy. But no lecture lists the contraindications to endoscopy, so the reasons given for A, B, C and E are from general principles. Verify them before relying on them.

resp-w6-new-q13-13:
From 05 - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory System. Each muscle acts on either the cricothyroid joint (pitch) or the cricoarytenoid joint (opening and closing):

  • A – iv: cricothyroid tilts the cricothyroid joint to lengthen the cords (↑ pitch). It is the only one supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
  • B – v: vocalis/thyroarytenoid shorten the cords (↓ pitch).
  • C – iii: posterior cricoarytenoid rotates the vocal processes laterally. It is the only abductor.
  • D – ii: lateral cricoarytenoid rotates them medially, a pivot adduction.
  • E – i: interarytenoid slides the arytenoids together, a translational adduction synergistic with D.
  • F – vi: aryepiglottic pulls the epiglottis down to close the inlet in swallowing.

resp-w7-new-q15-15.html:
From 07 - Cystic Fibrosis and the CF column of 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. Check each statement against the notes:

  • A: both notes place the CFTR gene on the long arm of chromosome 7 (7q), not the short arm. As written, A is false.
  • B: true. ΔF508, a 3-base-pair deletion that loses phenylalanine 508, is the commonest mutation (70–80%).
  • C: true. The chart gives about 2000 known mutations.
  • D: true in substance. CFTR normally secretes Cl− in the airway and gut, and the defective channel cannot.

On the notes, B, C and D are true and A is false, so “all of the above” cannot stand.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: Option A puts the CF gene on the short arm of chromosome 7. Both 07 - Cystic Fibrosis and the CF column of 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease put it on the long arm (7q). That makes A false and “All of the above” (E) indefensible. Either A was mistranscribed (“long” to “short”) or the key is wrong. No other option works on its own, since B, C and D are each true.

resp-w7-new-q4-4.html:
From the Rhinology chart in 07 - Radiology (Week 7), which carries the acute rhinosinusitis column that 09 - Acute Rhinosinusitis lacks. The chart lists the referral red flags for ABRS as systemic toxicity, altered mental status, severe headache, and orbital swelling or reduced visual acuity. They signal spread beyond the sinus: orbital cellulitis, or intracranial extension such as meningitis, abscess or cavernous sinus thrombosis. Otherwise the default is watchful waiting for 7–10 days with INCS and saline.

  • A, B, C are each on the list.
  • D (A and C): leaves out altered mental status.
  • E: the only complete answer.

resp-w8-new-q1-1.html:
From In Class - Epistaxis and 05 - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory System. Posterior bleeds arise at Woodruff's plexus, where the sphenopalatine artery (maxillary artery, external carotid) enters the posterior nasal cavity. They drip down the throat, are rarely traumatic, are worse than anterior bleeds and cluster in elderly hypertensive patients. When packing fails, the surgical fix is sphenopalatine artery ligation.

  • B (facial artery): reaches the nose through the superior labial branch at the anterior septum (Kiesselbach's).
  • C (anterior ethmoid): supplies the anterior-superior cavity and also feeds Kiesselbach's. It is an internal-carotid branch, so IR must not embolise it.
  • D (ophthalmic artery): the parent of both ethmoid arteries, supplying the roof rather than the posterior cavity.

review.t: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory System

resp-w8-new-q2-2.html:
From In Class - Epistaxis and the stepwise plan in 07 - Radiology. Most bleeds are anterior, from Kiesselbach's plexus, and the lecture's first-aid step is to pinch the soft ala firmly for 10–15 minutes, head tipped forward to protect the airway. After ABCs and reversing coagulopathy, this is the first treatment on the ladder, and it stops most low-volume bleeds on its own.

  • B (cautery): step 4, for a visible vessel that keeps bleeding after pressure. It is unilateral silver nitrate.
  • A (packing): step 5, when pressure and cautery fail.
  • E (tranexamic acid): a topical hemostatic at step 6, used alongside packing.
  • C (embolization): the last step, for refractory bleeding. The note adds that it needs active bleeding to work.

resp-w8-new-q3-3.html:
From the epistaxis chart and stepwise plan in 07 - Radiology, and In Class - Epistaxis. When bleeding continues despite packing, the surgical step is to ligate the anterior ethmoid and sphenopalatine arteries. Those two cover the internal- and external-carotid supply to the nose, so E is appropriate for severe bleeding.

  • A: interventional radiology embolizes external carotid branches, not the anterior ethmoid. That is an internal carotid (ophthalmic) branch, so embolizing it risks the eye and brain.
  • B: the plan specifies unilateral silver nitrate cautery. Cauterizing both sides of the thin septum risks a septal perforation (general principle; the notes only say unilateral).
  • C: posterior packs are rare, used mostly in elderly patients, and are not left unmonitored. The notes do not spell this out; it follows from the airway risk.
  • D: juvenile nasal angiofibroma is highly vascular. The chart says do NOT biopsy because of the risk of hemorrhage.

resp-w8-new-q4-4.html:
From 01 - Hemoptysis, with 02 - Pneumonia. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is the vasculitis most likely to cavitate. As a systemic disease it brings extrapulmonary features: the history asks about bleeding from the nose, ears and urinary tract. D is true.

  • A: the lecture's main cause of cavitary disease is tuberculosis, then fungi (Aspergillus in immunocompromised patients) and vasculitis. The Pneumonia note also lists anaerobic and pyogenic bacteria and NTM. "Fungal or non-tuberculosis" leaves out the most common cause.
  • B: cavities belong to secondary (reactivation) TB at the apices. Primary TB gives a nonspecific lower-lobe infiltrate and hilar nodes.
  • C: this is backwards. In diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (capillaritis), serial lavage gets more bloody with each wash. Returns that clear point towards pneumonia.

resp-w8-new-q5-5.html:
From 01 - Hemoptysis, with the bronchiectasis column in 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. Bronchiectasis is permanent airway dilation after repeated infection or inflammation. Its causes include diffuse ones (CF, primary ciliary dyskinesia) and focal ones (an obstructing foreign body or tumour). The exam finding is localized crackles and the CXR findings are nonspecific, so "only diffuse" is false.

  • A (true): bronchitis is a diagnosis of exclusion, made after other infectious, parenchymal and alveolar causes are ruled out. The CXR is usually normal.
  • B (true): bleeding comes from damage to inflamed airways. Capillary leakage is more likely on blood thinners or with a smoking history.
  • C (true): repeated insults destroy the bronchial walls. This is why bronchiectasis is the most common cause of rapid, life-threatening hemoptysis.

resp-w8-new-q6-6.html:
From the epistaxis chart in 07 - Radiology, and In Class - Epistaxis. The chart splits causes into local (trauma, foreign body, tumour, cocaine, inflammation, barometric change, nasal dryness) and systemic (coagulopathy, hypertension, atherosclerosis, HHT, GPA). Barometric pressure changes act on the nasal mucosa itself, so D is the local cause and is not systemic.

  • A (hypertension): systemic. The in-class note lists essential hypertension and targets it in outpatient care.
  • B (coagulopathy): systemic. Reversing it is step 2 of management.
  • C (HHT): systemic. It is autosomal dominant, with malformed vessels in the nose and lungs.
  • E: fails because D is a local cause.

resp-w8-new-q7-7.html:
From the stepwise plan in 07 - Radiology and In Class - Epistaxis. Epistaxis treatment is pressure, cautery, packing, hemostatics, then surgery or IR. Nasal irrigation is not on that ladder. Saline irrigation is a treatment for acute and chronic rhinosinusitis, and outpatient epistaxis advice is humidity and moisture, not flushing. Irrigation would also dislodge the clot you are trying to keep.

  • B and C (tampon, packing): the same step. The note calls a nasal pack "basically a tampon for the nasal cavity"; ribbon gauze and posterior packs are the alternatives.
  • D (tranexamic acid): a topical hemostatic, step 6.
  • E (pressure): first-line. Pinch the ala for 10–15 minutes, leaning forward.

resp-w8-new-q8-8.html:
From 04 - Approach to Pulmonary Nodules and Masses. Small nodules carry a significantly lower risk of malignancy. The chart calls solitary nodules under 7 mm likely benign: under 6 mm and low-risk needs no follow-up, while ≥ 8 mm gets CT at 3 months, PET/CT or sampling. So C is true. (The note's "< 8cm" in the PET paragraph is a typo for mm.)

  • A: solitary nodules are typically asymptomatic and found incidentally.
  • B: multiple nodules have a broad benign differential (histoplasmosis, TB, sarcoidosis, vasculitis, pneumoconiosis). When malignant, they usually mean metastasis.
  • D: the aim is the opposite. Pick one biopsy site that gives stage and diagnosis in a single procedure.
  • E: M0 means no distant metastasis; M1 indicates metastasis.

resp-w7-new-q11-11.html:
From the restrictive-disease chart in 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease and 05 - Interstitial Causes of Dyspnea. The prognosis row for IPF reads: rapid progression, mean survival 4–5 years, respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale. All three follow one chain. Fibrosis thickens the barrier and stiffens the lung, and gas exchange fails. Chronic hypoxia constricts the pulmonary arterioles and the scarring destroys the capillary bed, producing pulmonary hypertension. The right ventricle then fails against that pressure, which is cor pulmonale. So E.

  • D (A and B): leaves out cor pulmonale, the end of the same chain.
  • A, B, C alone: each is true but incomplete.

resp-w7-new-q7-7.html:
Partly from the larynx section of Summary Notes - Anatomy. The anatomy notes cover the structure: the vocal ligament is covered by mucosa to form the vocal folds, the lateral cricoarytenoid adducts them, and the cricothyroid tenses them to raise pitch. Voice needs three things together:

  • A: the folds approximate (adduct) so that they close the glottis.
  • B: an expiratory airflow builds subglottic pressure beneath the closed folds.
  • C: that airflow sets the mucosal free edge passively vibrating. No muscle contracts for each cycle.

Remove any one and voice fails: open folds give a breathy voice, too little airflow gives no sound, and stiff scarred mucosa gives hoarseness. That makes E the answer. "Forced" overstates B, since conversational speech needs a controlled expiratory stream, not a forced one.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: The anatomy notes cover vocal-fold structure and adduction, but no lecture note covers the airflow and mucosal-vibration mechanism of phonation; that part is reasoned from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

gu-w14-new-q11-11:
From 13 - IV Fluids. The lecture's own (non-exhaustive) list of indications names every option: ECF hypovolemia (restore hemodynamics and tissue perfusion), ICF hypovolemia (free water to re-expand shrunken cells), replacing deficits and ongoing losses, nutrition in certain instances, and correcting electrolyte and acid-base disturbances.

  • E (A, B and D) is the trap: it leaves out nutrition, which the lecture lists as a valid (if less common) reason.
  • Each of A to D alone is true but incomplete, so F is the only full answer.
gu-w14-new-q22-22:
From 06 - Reabsorption and Secretion. The thick ascending limb reabsorbs about 30% of the remaining filtered NaCl through the apical Na-K-2Cl cotransporter, and it is impermeable to water, which is how it dilutes the filtrate and builds the hypertonic medulla.

  • A: true; NKCC moves Na, K and Cl in, and the K back-leak drives paracellular Ca and Mg reabsorption.
  • B: true; water-impermeable.
  • C: true ("look" is a typo for loop); furosemide blocks NKCC.
  • D: false; the distal tubule's transporter is the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter, not NKCC.

So E.
gu-wb-gu0-q22:
From 06 - Reabsorption and Secretion and 12 - Potassium Handling by the Kidney. Net K+ secretion happens in the cortical collecting duct, by the principal cells: Na+ enters through ENaC, leaving the lumen negative, which pulls K+ out into the urine. The lecture puts 90-95% of the body's ability to excrete K+ here, and aldosterone turns it up.

  • PCT: bulk reabsorption of Na, water, glucose and HCO3, not K+ secretion.
  • Descending limb: water-permeable, little solute transport.
  • DCT: Na-Cl cotransport and active Ca reabsorption.
  • Medullary collecting duct: the lectures place K+ regulation in the cortical segment.

gu-wb-gu0-q23.html:
From 12 - Potassium Handling by the Kidney. Alkalosis moves K+ into cells: the lecture lists metabolic alkalosis among the causes of shift into cells (a small effect), and the opposite of metabolic acidosis, which is listed under shift out of cells.

  • Digoxin overdose, beta blockers and lack of insulin (undiagnosed type 1 diabetes) are each named under "shift out of cells (or lack of cellular uptake)".
  • Hyperosmolarity is not in the lecture note. By general principle, water leaving cells raises intracellular K+ and drags it out with it (solvent drag), which is why hyperglycemia itself raises serum K+.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: The hyperosmolarity distractor is not covered by the lecture note; its rationale is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

gu-wb-gu0-q27:
From 13 - IV Fluids. The lecture sorts IV fluids by what is dissolved in the water. Crystalloids are water with electrolytes and/or glucose; colloids are water with albumin, plasma or large carbohydrates (starches, dextran), which stay in the plasma and pull fluid in from the interstitium.

  • 5% albumin is a colloid, so it is the odd one out.
  • D5W (dextrose in water, effectively free water), normal saline, 3% hypertonic saline and Ringer's lactate are all crystalloids, differing only in their salt and glucose content.

gu-wb-gu0-q85.html:
From 05 - Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum. The lecture places the apertures as: vena caval foramen at T8 (IVC, right phrenic nerve), esophageal hiatus at T10 (esophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks), and aortic hiatus at T12 (aorta, thoracic duct, azygos). Its mnemonic "I ate (8) ten (10) eggs at twelve (12)" reads IVC 8, Esophagus 10, Aorta 12.

The stem asks in the order esophagus, IVC, aorta, which gives T10, T8, T12: option B.

  • A lists the levels in mnemonic order (IVC first), not in the stem's order.
  • C and D misplace the aorta or all three.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives A (T8, T10, T12), but the stem lists the structures as esophagus, IVC, aorta. 05 - Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum puts the esophagus at T10 and the IVC at T8, so the answer in the stem's order is B (T10, T8, T12). The key's own mnemonic supports B.

reviews-gu-Q2:
From 06 - Reabsorption and Secretion. The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs 100% of filtered glucose (and amino acids), coupled to Na+ entry through Na-glucose cotransporters on its brush border. That is why SGLT2 inhibitors act here, and why Fanconi syndrome, a PCT defect, shows up as glucosuria.

  • Descending limb: water-permeable, almost no solute transport.
  • Ascending limb: NaCl via NKCC, no glucose.
  • DCT: Na-Cl cotransport and Ca reabsorption.
  • Collecting duct: Na via ENaC, K+/H+ secretion and ADH-regulated water; by then no glucose is left to reclaim.
reviews-gu-Q5:
From 08 - Diuretics and 02 - Nephrolithiasis. Thiazides block the Na-Cl cotransporter in the DCT; Na+ can then enter only through the Na-Ca exchanger, so Ca2+ reabsorption rises and urinary Ca falls. The lecture calls this what makes thiazides a treatment for calcium stones with hypercalciuria.

  • A (loop diuretic): loops increase urinary Ca by abolishing the positive lumen charge that drives paracellular Ca reabsorption, which worsens stones.
  • C: stopping diuretics does nothing for the hypercalciuria.
  • D: potassium-sparing agents act on the collecting duct and have no stated calcium effect.
  • E: the Nephrolithiasis note says low calcium intake predisposes to stones; keep intake normal.
reviews-gu-Q6:
From 08 - Diuretics and 06 - Reabsorption and Secretion. Amiloride and triamterene block ENaC on principal cells of the collecting duct. With less Na+ entering, the lumen stays less negative, so K+ is not pulled into the urine: modest natriuresis with K+ retention. Spironolactone reaches the same channel indirectly, by blocking aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor.

  • A is the loop diuretic target (NKCC, thick ascending limb).
  • B is the thiazide target (NCC, DCT).
  • D and E describe what increases K+ secretion (aldosterone up-regulates ENaC and Na/K ATPase), the opposite of sparing potassium.
reviews-gu-Q7:
From 11 - Acid Base Disturbances. pH 7.29 is acidemia, and the HCO3 is low (14), so the primary process is metabolic acidosis. Check compensation with the lecture's 1:1 rule for metabolic acidosis: HCO3 has fallen 10 (24 to 14), so pCO2 should fall about 10 (40 to 30). It is 30, so the respiratory response is appropriate and no second disorder is needed.

  • Respiratory acidosis needs a high pCO2; here it is low.
  • Respiratory or metabolic alkalosis and mixed alkalosis need a pH above 7.45. The low pCO2 is compensation, not a primary alkalosis.

gu-w15-new-q11-11.html:
From 05 - Chronic Kidney Disease and 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. The CKD lecture gives the indications for dialysis as AEIOU: Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalemia) or encephalopathy, "itis" (uremic pericarditis), Overload, Uremia. In CKD the decline is slow, and hyperkalemia, acidosis and volume are usually managed medically for a long time. What eventually forces dialysis is the uremic syndrome: anorexia, nausea, progressive malnutrition and cognitive change. The RRT lecture lists these as the elective indications.

  • Refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis and volume overload are urgent indications, more typical of AKI.
  • Pericarditis is urgent but uncommon.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: The notes list the AEIOU indications but never rank them, so "most common" is reasoned from general principles, not from a lecture. Verify it before relying on it.

gu-w15-new-q14-14.html:
From 05 - Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum and Summary Notes - Anatomy (duodenum). The lecture's GI retroperitoneal list is the duodenum, pancreas, ascending colon, descending colon and rectum. The sigmoid colon is not on it: it hangs on its own mesentery (the sigmoid mesocolon) and is intraperitoneal.

  • A (2/3 of the duodenum): the anatomy summary makes parts 2-4 of the duodenum retroperitoneal; only the first (superior) part is intraperitoneal.
  • B, C, D are on the retroperitoneal list directly.

gu-w15-new-q15-15.html:
From 05 - Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum. The lecture's three apertures and their contents: the caval opening (T8) carries the IVC and the right phrenic nerve; the esophageal hiatus (T10) carries the esophagus and the anterior and posterior vagal trunks; the aortic hiatus (T12) carries the aorta, the thoracic duct and the azygos system ("I ate 10 eggs at 12").

  • A and B swap the contents: the vagal trunks go with the esophagus, the right phrenic nerve with the IVC.
  • C is the only correct pairing.

gu-w15-new-q18-18:
From 02 - Measurement of Renal Function. BUN depends on how much urea is made and how much is reabsorbed, not just on GFR. The lecture's BUN:Cr table puts GI bleeding (a protein load digested from blood) and heart failure (hypoperfusion; a sodium-avid kidney reabsorbs urea with Na) in the high-ratio, pre-renal row.

  • Corticosteroids are not in the table. They raise BUN by increasing protein catabolism, the same mechanism as a high protein load.
  • Protein malnutrition and cirrhosis sit in the low-ratio row: less protein or less hepatic urea synthesis means a lower BUN.
gu-wb-gu0-q94:
From 03 - Hematuria and Proteinuria and 08 - Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology. Nephritic syndrome is glomerular inflammation: hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts, a modest amount of proteinuria, oliguria, and fluid retention with hypertension and edema. Hyperlipidemia belongs to nephrotic syndrome: the liver over-produces lipoproteins as it tries to replace the albumin lost in massive proteinuria.

  • B, E: the lecture's markers of glomerular hematuria (RBC casts; 70% or more dysmorphic RBCs).
  • C: proteinuria is present but below the nephrotic range.
  • D: hypertension from salt and water retention.

gu-w16-meds2024-q5-5.html:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Pelvis. Each hip bone (os coxae) is three fused bones: the ilium, ischium and pubis, which meet at the acetabulum. The two hip bones meet anteriorly at the pubic symphysis and join the sacrum posteriorly; with the coccyx they make up the bony pelvis.

  • Femur, tibia: bones of the lower limb, not the pelvis.
  • Ileum (with an e) is the small bowel; ilium (with an i) is the bone, a classic spelling trap.
  • Symphysis is the joint between the two pubic bones, not a bone.
  • Coccyx is part of the pelvis but not of the hip bone.

gu-wb-gu0-q116:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. A varicocele is a dilated network of gonadal veins, the pampiniform plexus, from back-flow (raised abdominal pressure or defective gonadal vein valves). It feels like a "bag of worms".

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.
gu-wb-gu0-q117:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. A hematocele is blood between the layers of the tunica vaginalis, almost always after trauma, and may involve testicular rupture; scrotal ultrasound confirms it and rules rupture out. The contrast to learn is with a hydrocele: the same space, filled with fluid rather than blood, and it transilluminates.

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.
gu-wb-gu0-q118:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. In testicular torsion the gubernaculum fails to anchor the testis, which lies horizontally and can swing and twist on its cord. It presents as sudden severe pain in adolescents and young adults, with a rock-hard testis (arterial inflow, no venous outflow), and needs surgery within 6-8 hours.

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.
gu-wb-gu0-q119:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. An adult hydrocele is fluid in the enclosed space lined by the tunica vaginalis (in infants it is usually a hernia sac communicating with the peritoneum). It transilluminates, and you can get "above" it on pinching the top of the scrotum, which a hernia does not allow. Blood in the same space would be a hematocele.

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.
gu-wb-gu0-q120:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. A spermatocele is a multilocular, semen-filled sac from a seminal fluid leak off the epididymis. It feels like a "third testicle" and is seldom symptomatic unless large.

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.
gu-wb-gu0-q121:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. Orchitis is infection of the testis, and the lecture presents it with the epididymis as epididymo-orchitis. Unlike torsion, the pain is usually gradual, Doppler shows blood flow, and there are signs of infection (fever, raised WBC). It is treated with antibiotics, not surgery.

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.
gu-wb-gu0-q123:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. In an indirect inguinal hernia bowel protrudes through the inguinal canal and can reach the scrotum, where it mimics a hydrocele. Pinch the top of the scrotum: you cannot get above a hernia, but you can get above a hydrocele.

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.
gu-w17-new-q10-10:
From 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. The AV fistula is the optimal access. A permcath is simply a tunnelled line into the internal jugular, and catheters carry the highest infection risk, so ease of set-up does not make it optimal.

  • A: true; pericarditis and uncontrollable fluid overload are urgent indications.
  • B: true; anorexia and GFR <5 mL/min are elective indications.
  • D: true; with a machine, training and tested home water, patients can dialyse at home.
gu-w17-new-q11-11:
From 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. As with hemodialysis, most patients on peritoneal dialysis eventually die of cardiovascular disease. That is the sense in which it is the "main" complication: peritonitis is the commoner acute one.

  • A: PD is less expensive than hemodialysis and home-based.
  • B: the filter is the patient's own peritoneum, not skin. Hypertonic glucose dialysate draws fluid across it by osmosis.
  • C: it increases patient autonomy.

gu-wb-gu0-q29.html: From 05 - Chronic Kidney Disease. True. The lecture ranks the major causes of CKD as #1 diabetes (diabetic nephropathy), #2 essential hypertension, #3 glomerulonephritis, with polycystic kidney disease the commonest genetic cause of ESRD. The Renal Replacement Therapies lecture adds that rising type 2 diabetes is driving the growth in chronic dialysis. The statement concerns chronic renal failure. For acute kidney injury the commonest renal cause is tubular injury (ATN), not diabetes.

gu-w15-new-q10-10.html:
From 06 - Diabetic Nephropathy and 05 - Chronic Kidney Disease. The lipid target is LDL <2, so an LDL of 4 is not a goal; it is hyperlipidemia left untreated.

  • A: 130/80 is the BP target in diabetic patients (<140/80 in non-diabetics), usually with an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
  • B: protein restriction is advised only for those already on a high-protein diet. High protein dilates the afferent arteriole and raises glomerular pressure.
  • D: tight glycemic control, HbA1c <7%.

gu-w15-new-q19-19.html:
From 02 - Measurement of Renal Function. The lecture's contraindications include a solitary kidney (a bleed could cost the only kidney) and end-stage renal disease (small scarred kidneys; the diagnosis no longer changes management). The others on the list are an uncooperative patient, coagulopathy, severe uncontrolled hypertension, severe anemia, cystic kidney, hydronephrosis, acute pyelonephritis, renal artery aneurysms and suspected cancer.

  • B: a transplanted kidney is not a contraindication. In general it is biopsied routinely to diagnose rejection, even though it is a single kidney.
  • D: hyperkalemia is not on the list.

gu-wb-gu0-q106.html:
From 02 - Measurement of Renal Function. The lecture says WBCs in the urine should make you think of UTI first, especially with bacteria on microscopy; interstitial nephritis is the other cause. What separates the two is whether the WBCs are free or packed into casts.

  • A: glomerulonephritis gives RBC casts.
  • B: hyaline casts are the nonspecific, possibly normal finding.
  • C: ATN gives muddy brown granular casts.
  • E: AIN needs WBC casts, not free WBCs.

gu-wb-gu0-q107.html:
From 02 - Measurement of Renal Function. A cast forms in the tubule, from Tamm-Horsfall protein precipitating in the distal tubule and collecting duct. WBCs wrapped in that protein therefore localize the inflammation to the kidney itself, and the lecture links WBC casts to interstitial nephritis. The AKI lecture pairs sterile pyuria and WBC casts with drug-induced AIN.

  • D: a lower UTI gives free WBCs and bacteria, not casts.
  • A: RBC casts; C: muddy brown casts; B: hyaline casts.

gu-wb-gu0-q109.html:
From 04 - Acute Kidney Injury. Muddy brown granular casts are made of sloughed, necrotic tubular epithelium, and the lecture ties them to ATN, the commonest renal cause of AKI (ischemic or nephrotoxic). They contrast with the hyaline casts and low FENa of pre-renal AKI.

  • A: glomerulonephritis gives RBC casts.
  • B: hyaline casts are the nonspecific finding.
  • D: UTI gives free WBCs and bacteria.
  • E: AIN gives WBC casts.

gu-wb-gu0-q122.html:
From 09 - Special Issues in Pediatric Urology. Cryptorchidism is failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum: 3% of term and 30% of premature infants. Most descend within 3-6 months; orchidopexy by 17 months if not. Untreated, it raises cancer risk 3-8x, and bilateral cases compromise fertility.

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.

gu-w17-new-q13-13.html:
From 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. True. The lecture's transplant complications are rejection, surgical anastomotic problems, infection (CMV, herpes), cancer from immunosuppression (lymphoma, skin cancer), cardiovascular disease, and drug side effects. Calcineurin inhibitors cause hypertension, hyperlipidemia and CKD, and the immunosuppressants can cause diabetes and bone disease. The original disease can also recur in the graft.

The underlying trade-off is between too much immunosuppression (infection, cancer) and too little (rejection).
